{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Walter Helbig Gottschalk''' (November 3, 1918 – February 15, 2004) was an American mathematician, one of the founders of [[topological dynamics]].

==Biography==
Gottschalk was born in [[Lynchburg, Virginia]], on November 3, 1918, and moved to [[Salem, Virginia]] as a child.<ref name="gestalts">[http://gottschalksgestalts.org/aboutauth.html About the author] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160309140948/http://gottschalksgestalts.org/aboutauth.html |date=2016-03-09 }}, Gottschalk's Gestalts, retrieved 2012-11-21.</ref><ref name="salem">[http://www.sefandaa.org/halloffame/gottschalkw.html Walter H. Gottschalk] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150203051516/http://www.sefandaa.org/halloffame/gottschalkw.html |date=2015-02-03 }}, Salem Educational Foundation and Alumni Association Hall of Fame, retrieved 2012-11-21.</ref> His father, Carl Gottschalk, 
was a German immigrant who worked as a machinist and later owned several small businesses in Salem; his younger brother, [[Carl W. Gottschalk]], became a notable medical researcher.<ref>{{citation|title=Carl W. Gottschalk|journal=Biographical Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=77|pages=122–141|year=1999|url=http://www.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=9681&page=122}}</ref>

Gottschalk did both his undergraduate studies and graduate studies at the [[University of Virginia]], finishing with a Ph.D. in 1944 under the supervision of [[Gustav A. Hedlund]].<ref name="gestalts"/><ref name="salem"/><ref name="mg">{{mathgenealogy|name=Walter Helbig Gottschalk|id=36254}}</ref> After graduating, he joined the faculty of the [[University of Pennsylvania]], and was chair of the Pennsylvania mathematics department from 1954 to 1958.<ref name="gestalts"/><ref name="salem"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.math.upenn.edu/History/tenured_faculty_1899-.html|title=Tenured faculty 1899–|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130106234657/http://www.math.upenn.edu/History/tenured_faculty_1899-.html|archive-date=2013-01-06 }} {{cite web|url=http://www.math.upenn.edu/History/dept_chairs.html|title=Past department chairs|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305215314/https://www.math.upenn.edu/History/dept_chairs.html|archive-date=2016-03-05|publisher=Univ. of Pennsylvania Dept. of Mathematics}}</ref> In the academic year 1947/1948 he was a visiting scholar at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>[http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/users/4592 Gottschalk, Walter H., Institute for Advanced Study]</ref> At Pennsylvania, his doctoral students included [[Philip Rabinowitz (mathematician)|Philip Rabinowitz]], who became known for his work in [[numerical analysis]], and [[Robert Ellis (mathematician)|Robert Ellis]], who became known for his work on topological dynamics.<ref name="mg"/> Gottschalk moved to [[Wesleyan University]] in 1963; at Wesleyan, he also served two terms as chair before retiring in 1982.<ref name="gestalts"/><ref name="salem"/> He died on February 15, 2004, in [[Providence, Rhode Island]], where he had lived since his retirement.<ref name="gestalts"/>

==Contributions==
Gottschalk and his advisor Gustav Hedlund wrote the 1955 monograph ''Topological Dynamics''.<ref name="gestalts"/><ref>Review of ''Topological Dynamics'' by Y. N. Dowker, {{MR|0074810}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Halmos | first = Paul R. | author-link = Paul Halmos
 | doi = 10.1090/S0002-9904-1955-09999-3
 | issue = 6
 | journal = Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society
 | mr = 1565733
 | pages = 584–588
 | title = Book Review: W. H. Gottschalk and G. A. Hedlund, ''Topological dynamics''
 | volume = 61
 | year = 1955| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> Other research contributions of Gottschalk include the first study of [[surjunctive group]]s{{sfnp|Gottschalk|1973}} and a short proof of the [[De Bruijn–Erdős theorem (graph theory)|De Bruijn–Erdős theorem]] on [[graph coloring|coloring]] infinite graphs.{{sfnp|Gottschalk|1951}}

As well as being a research mathematician, Gottschalk also put on two exhibits of mathematical sculptures in the 1960s.<ref name="gestalts"/>

==Awards and honors==
Gottschalk was a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name="gestalts"/>
